name: Eval Datasets
question: Is the test set itself worth trusting?
summary: Build and maintain the set of cases every other evaluation runs on. Cases come from production logs, support tickets and subject experts; they are stratified by intent, language and risk, topped up with edge, adversarial and reviewed synthetic cases, labelled against a rubric by two people, sized for the confidence you need, versioned, and refreshed from new failures. The scoring methods live in the other techniques here; this one is about the data they score.
useCases: Before trusting any release gate, judge or benchmark comparison on your own tasks
When scores look good but users still report failures the set never shows
When a new language, intent or product line reaches production

steps.title: Start from real traffic
steps.text: Sample six months of the claims assistant's conversations, plus support tickets and the cases claims officers say go wrong. Redact names, phone numbers, policy numbers and Aadhaar numbers before anyone reads them. The helpers here (load_logs, redact, label and so on) are stubs for your own code.

steps.title: Stratify, with a floor
steps.text: Group the logs by intent, language and risk, and sample each group in proportion to its traffic, but never fewer than 3 cases. Proportional sampling alone would give a 1% intent such as a death claim about 2 cases out of 180; the floor keeps rare but costly intents in the set.

steps.title: Fill gaps carefully
steps.text: Where a stratum has fewer than 3 real cases, synthetic cases fill the gap, and each is kept only if a subject expert approves it. 20 adversarial cases are added on purpose: a claim PDF with hidden instructions, a claim number that does not exist, abusive Hinglish. They are scored as their own slice.

steps.title: Label twice, then adjudicate
steps.text: Two annotators grade all 200 cases against the same written rubric. They disagree on 24: 88% agreement, but Cohen's κ is only about 0.53, because most answers are correct and agreement on those is easy. A senior claims officer settles each disagreement, and unclear rubric lines are rewritten.

steps.title: Size for the margin you need
steps.text: At 85% accuracy on 180 production-like cases the 95% margin is 1.96 × √(0.85 × 0.15 ÷ 180) ≈ ±5.2 points. A real 4-point regression disappears inside that. Comparing two versions needs more, about 900 cases for a margin of ±2.3 on each score.

steps.title: Version, hold out, refresh
steps.text: Save the set as v4 with the labels, and keep a fifth of it as a holdout that nobody looks at while tuning prompts. Every month, add the new production failures, so the set follows the traffic instead of last year's.

pros: Every other evaluation becomes trustworthy only on a set that looks like real traffic
Stratification shows weak slices, such as Hindi or rare intents, that an average hides
Two annotators and a rubric turn fuzzy judgments into labels you can defend
A versioned, refreshed set lets you compare releases fairly over time
cons: Annotator time is the main cost: two labellers plus adjudication roughly doubles it
Production logs need redaction and consent checks under DPDP before use
Detecting small changes needs hundreds to thousands of cases
A set tuned against repeatedly stops predicting real performance
avoidWhen: A throwaway prototype where a dozen hand-picked cases are enough to spot obvious breaks
Comparing general model capability before you have any traffic (start with public benchmarks)

playgroundGuide.scenario: Suraksha General, a fictional Indian insurer, runs a claims assistant that is right about 85% of the time on real traffic. Traffic spans 12 intents, and 20% of it is in Hindi or Hinglish. The next release is truly 4 points worse: Hindi answers drop 15 points and the new flood-claim intent drops 20. You design the test set and see whether it can tell.
controls: Choose how many cases the set holds: 50, 200 or 1,000.
Choose where cases come from and how they are labelled: one annotator, or two plus adjudication.
Turn on the monthly refresh from new production failures, or load a scenario.

outputs.name: Measured accuracy
outputs.meaning: The score the set reports, with its 95% margin, 1.96 × √(p(1 − p) ÷ n).

outputs.name: Intents covered
outputs.meaning: How many of the 12 real intents have at least 3 cases in the set.

outputs.name: Hindi / Hinglish cases
outputs.meaning: How many cases are in the Hindi slice, and that slice's own margin.

outputs.name: Label noise
outputs.meaning: The share of gold labels that are wrong, and the labelling hours it took.

outputs.name: 4-point regression detected
outputs.meaning: Whether the measured drop is larger than the margin for a difference between two scores.

presets.name: 50 synthetic, one annotator
presets.expect: 94% ± 6.6 points, but only 6 of 12 intents and no Hindi. The regression shows as 0.00 points: missed.

presets.name: 200 from production, one annotator
presets.expect: 85% ± 4.9, 9 of 12 intents, 40 Hindi cases, 12% label noise. The drop shows as 2.28 points against ±7.0: missed.

presets.name: 200 stratified, two annotators, refresh
presets.expect: All 12 intents, 50 Hindi cases, 20 adversarial, 3% noise, 22 hours of labelling. The drop shows as 3.76 against ±7.4: still missed.

presets.name: 1,000 stratified, two annotators, refresh
presets.expect: 85% ± 2.3 on 900 scored cases, 250 Hindi cases, 110 hours. The drop shows as 3.76 against ±3.3: detected.

missions.text: Build a set that detects the real 4-point regression.
missions.hint: You need 1,000 real cases, two annotators so the drop is not shrunk by noise, and the refresh so the flood-claim failures are in the set.

practice.scenario: Suraksha General, a fictional Indian insurer, first tested its claims assistant on 50 questions an LLM generated from the FAQ, and it scored 94%. The rebuilt set samples real conversations, stratified by the 12 intents, Hindi and English, and risk, with a floor of 3 cases per stratum and 10% adversarial cases. Two annotators label every case against a rubric and a senior claims officer settles disagreements. Accuracy on the new set is 85%, with a margin wide enough to show why 1,000 cases are needed before a 4-point regression becomes visible. Each month's new failures are added to the next version.

industries.use: Claims and policy-servicing assistants tested on real claims, stratified by product, language and claim size
UPI dispute and card-block assistants tested with fraud-style adversarial cases and a held-back slice
Triage and discharge-summary assistants labelled by two clinicians, with disagreements adjudicated

practice.analogy: An exam paper for a driving licence. If every question is about parking on a sunny day, a pass tells you nothing about night driving in the rain. A good paper samples every road condition, is marked by two examiners, and changes each year so nobody learns the answers.

library.name: statsmodels
library.what: Statistics library with confidence intervals and sample-size calculations for proportions, used here with pandas for stratified sampling and scikit-learn for Cohen’s κ.

practice.note: The log export and column names are illustrative. proportion_confint and samplesize_confint_proportion are real statsmodels functions; the Wilson interval behaves better than the plain normal formula when accuracy is near 0% or 100%.

samples.code:
import math
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.metrics import cohen_kappa_score
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_confint, samplesize_confint_proportion

logs = pd.read_parquet("claims_logs_redacted.parquet")   # intent, lang, risk, text

# 1. Stratified sample with a floor of 3 per stratum
TARGET, FLOOR = 900, 3
parts = []
for _, group in logs.groupby(["intent", "lang", "risk"]):
    k = max(FLOOR, round(TARGET * len(group) / len(logs)))
    parts.append(group.sample(min(k, len(group)), random_state=7))
sample = pd.concat(parts)
print(sample.groupby("lang").size())            # check the Hindi slice

# 2. Agreement between two annotators on the same cases
a = pd.read_csv("labels_a.csv")["verdict"]      # pass / fail per case
b = pd.read_csv("labels_b.csv")["verdict"]
print("agreement", (a == b).mean(), "kappa", round(cohen_kappa_score(a, b), 2))

# 3. How sure is the score? 765 of 900 correct = 85%
low, high = proportion_confint(count=765, nobs=900, alpha=0.05, method="wilson")
print(f"85.0% (95% CI {low:.1%} to {high:.1%})")

# 4. How many cases for a ±2-point margin at 85%?
n = samplesize_confint_proportion(proportion=0.85, half_length=0.02, alpha=0.05)
print(math.ceil(n))                              # 1,225 cases

numericDrill.question: Suraksha General’s claims assistant scores about 85% on real traffic. How many test cases are needed for a 95% margin of ±3 percentage points? Use n = 1.96² × p(1 − p) ÷ margin².
numericDrill.answer: n = 3.8416 × 0.85 × 0.15 ÷ 0.03² = 0.4898 ÷ 0.0009 ≈ 544.2, so round up to 545 cases. Halving the margin to ±1.5 points needs four times as many, about 2,177.

interview.question: How would you build an evaluation dataset for a production agent?
interview.answer: Sample real traffic, tickets and cases subject experts flag, after redacting personal data. Stratify by intent, language and risk with a minimum per stratum, and add edge and adversarial cases; use synthetic cases only to fill gaps, after expert review. Label with a written rubric, two annotators on at least a sample, measure agreement and adjudicate. Size it for the margin you need, version it, keep a holdout, and add new production failures every cycle.

interview.question: Your agent went from 84% to 87% on a 150-case test set. Is it better?
interview.answer: Not provably. At about 85% and 150 cases, one score has a margin near ±5.7 points, and the difference between two scores about ±8. A 3-point gain is inside that. Check paired results on the same cases, look at which cases flipped, and add cases, especially in the slices that matter, before claiming a win.

mistakes.mistake: Testing only on synthetic questions generated from documentation
mistakes.fix: Sample real production traffic, stratify it, and keep synthetic cases to reviewed gap-fillers

mistakes.mistake: Tuning prompts against the same test set until the score rises
mistakes.fix: Keep a holdout you never tune on, and refresh the set with new failures each release

quiz.question: A claims assistant scores 94% on 50 questions an LLM generated from the FAQ, but 85% when sampled real conversations are graded. Which number should the release decision use?
options: 85%: it reflects the traffic the assistant actually sees
quiz.explanation: Generated questions tend to be easier and tidier than real ones. The score that predicts production is the one measured on production-like cases.

quiz.question: A card-dispute assistant is 90% accurate on 400 test cases. What is the approximate 95% margin?
Where should cases for a claims assistant’s test set come from? Select all that apply.
options: A redacted sample of production conversations
Support tickets and complaints about the assistant
Cases claims officers say are tricky or high-risk
Only questions the team wrote while building the prompt
quiz.explanation: Real traffic, complaints and expert knowledge each surface different failures. Questions written by the builders mirror what the prompt already handles.

quiz.question: A UPI help assistant’s fraud-report intent is 0.5% of traffic. With 200 cases sampled purely in proportion, how many fraud reports land in the set, and what should you do?
options: About 1; set a floor per stratum so it gets at least a few cases
None; fraud cases cannot be tested
quiz.explanation: 0.5% of 200 is 1 case, too few to score. A floor per stratum keeps rare but costly intents in the set; reweight when reporting the overall score.

quiz.question: Two nurses label triage answers. They agree on 90% of cases, and each marks 90% of cases as pass. What is Cohen’s κ, roughly?
quiz.explanation: Chance agreement = 0.9² + 0.1² = 0.82. κ = (0.90 − 0.82) ÷ (1 − 0.82) = 0.08 ÷ 0.18 ≈ 0.44: moderate, much weaker than 90% suggests.

quiz.question: A plan-change assistant moves from 82% to 85% on a 100-case test set. What can you conclude?
options: Not much: each score has a margin of about ±7 points
It is worse, because the set is small
quiz.explanation: 1.96 × √(0.85 × 0.15 ÷ 100) ≈ 0.07, so about ±7 points on each score. A 3-point change is well inside the noise.

quiz.question: Which are signs that a returns assistant has been overfitted to its test set? Select all that apply.
options: The test score rose 8 points over a month of prompt tweaks, but complaints did not fall
The prompt now contains phrases copied from specific test cases
A holdout nobody tuned on scores far lower than the main set
Scores on the main set and the holdout are within a point of each other
quiz.explanation: Gains that do not carry to a holdout or to users, and prompts that quote test cases, are classic overfitting. Matching holdout scores are a good sign.

quiz.question: Labels are wrong 10% of the time, at random. The new release is truly 5 points worse. Roughly what drop will the test set show?
quiz.explanation: With symmetric label noise e, a real difference shrinks by (1 − 2e) = 1 − 0.2 = 0.8, so 5 × 0.8 = 4 points. Noisy labels hide real changes.

quiz.question: An NBFC’s loan-query assistant is about 80% accurate. How many cases give a 95% margin of ±2.5 points?
A bank has only 2 real conversations about locker nominations. How should synthetic cases be used?
options: Replace the whole test set with synthetic cases
Generate a few for that stratum and keep only those a subject expert approves
Generate hundreds so the stratum dominates the score
quiz.explanation: Synthetic cases are useful gap-fillers when reviewed. They should not replace real traffic or distort the overall score.

quiz.question: Before annotators read production conversations from a hospital’s billing assistant, which fields should be redacted? Select all that apply.
options: The detected intent, such as “bill dispute”
Diagnosis details not needed to judge the answer
quiz.explanation: Remove personal and health details that labelling does not need, in line with DPDP expectations. The intent is what annotators are judging.

quiz.question: A wallet’s Hindi slice has 60 test cases and scores 80%. What is its 95% margin?
quiz.explanation: 1.96 × √(0.8 × 0.2 ÷ 60) = 1.96 × 0.0516 ≈ 0.101, about ±10.1 points. Slice scores need far more cases than the overall score suggests.

quiz.question: A customer reports that the assistant told her a flood claim needs a police report, which is wrong. After the prompt is fixed, what should happen to the case?
options: Label it and add it to the next test-set version, so the regression is caught if it returns
Add it to the prompt as an example only
quiz.explanation: Every production failure is a test case you know matters. Adding it, redacted and labelled, stops the same mistake returning unnoticed.

quiz.question: Why keep a holdout slice of the test set that nobody looks at while tuning prompts?
options: To check that improvements carry over to cases the team did not tune against
Holdouts are only needed for fine-tuning
quiz.explanation: Repeated tuning against the same cases overfits them. The untouched holdout shows whether a gain is real.

quiz.question: Which are useful adversarial cases for a claims assistant? Select all that apply.
options: A claim PDF with hidden text telling the assistant to approve the claim
A claim number that does not exist
A routine “what is my motor claim status?” question
quiz.explanation: Adversarial cases probe injection, invented facts and hostile users. A routine status query belongs in the ordinary stratified sample.

quiz.question: A test set of 150 cases gives a margin of about ±6 points. How many cases would give about ±3 points at the same accuracy?
quiz.explanation: The margin shrinks with √n, so halving it needs four times the cases: 150 × 4 = 600.

quiz.question: Two teams report 88% and 91% for the same assistant, but neither names the test-set version. What is the problem?
options: The numbers cannot be compared, because the sets may differ
The lower score must be wrong
Only the higher score should be published
quiz.explanation: A score means something only with the dataset version it came from. Version the set and log it with every result.

quiz.question: Two annotators disagree on 15% of discharge-summary cases. What is the best next step?
options: Have a senior clinician adjudicate each disagreement and clarify the rubric where it caused them
Drop all disputed cases from the set
quiz.explanation: Adjudication fixes the gold labels, and rewriting unclear rubric lines stops the same disagreements next time. Dropping disputed cases removes the hardest ones.

quiz.question: A set of 1,000 synthetic English cases reports 94% ± 1.5 points, yet misses a real regression in Hindi answers. Why?
options: The set is precise about the wrong questions: it has no Hindi cases
quiz.explanation: A narrow margin only means the estimate is stable for the cases in the set. If a slice is missing, no amount of precision will reveal failures there.

quiz.question: A stratified set is 75% English and 25% Hindi, but traffic is 80% English and 20% Hindi. English accuracy is 90% and Hindi 70%. What overall accuracy should you report for traffic?
quiz.explanation: Reweight to the traffic mix: 0.8 × 90% + 0.2 × 70% = 72% + 14% = 86%. The unweighted set average, 0.75 × 90% + 0.25 × 70% = 85%, understates it.
